Statement: Legal notice to the Delhi Police and X Corp. over takedown demands against IFF’s account

On 3 November 2026, X Corp. forwarded to us two “Illegal Content Reports” submitted in the name of the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), @delhipolice. The first, dated 31 October, sought removal of a post we published on 30 October and a post by @SFLCin. The second, dated 2 November, sought removal of 37 posts and the withholding of three accounts in their entirety,  @internetfreedom, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia, on the ground that they defame the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. The posts in question reproduce and comment on a legal notice that was sent to us. They are protected speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. We were given no notice before these reports were filed. We learnt of them only because X forwarded copies.

Today, through our counsel Advocate Abhik Chimni and his colleagues, we served a legal notice on the Delhi Police, with a copy to X Corp.

Our position is simple:

1. Defamation is a non-cognizable offence. The police cannot investigate it without a Magistrate’s order, and cognizance can be taken only on a complaint by the person aggrieved.

2. The reports cite no complaint, no FIR, no Magistrate’s order and no court order, even though the box for “enforcement of court order” was ticked. Under Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, an intermediary can be required to take down content only on a court order or a reasoned government notification. A web form with “hate speech”, “defamation”, “safety/security” and “court order” ticked against 40 URLs, with one sentence of reasons, is not that.

3. Whether something is defamatory is for a court to decide after hearing the author. A police officer cannot decide it himself and direct a platform to act on his decision. Demanding that three accounts be withheld in full is grossly disproportionate to any grievance stated.

We have called upon the Delhi Police to withdraw both reports or disclaim within seven days, to furnish us the complaint and authority on which they were made, and to confirm that no further takedown requests will be made on this matter. If they do not, we will approach the Delhi High Court under Article 226. We have also requested X Corp. to take no action on the reports pending their withdrawal or adjudication. 

We are grateful to Advocate Abhik Chimni and his team for representing us in this matter. Redacted copies of the notice are attached.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

In July 2020, the Indian Army directed its personnel to remove 89 mobile applications to mitigate intelligence leakage, digital espionage and cybersecurity threats.

📍 Applications Covered Under the Original Restrictions

💬 Messaging Platforms: WeChat, QQ, Kik, Viber, Hike and LINE.

❤️ Dating Applications: Tinder, Bumble, Hinge, Badoo, Happn and OkCupid.

🌐 Social Networking: Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat.

🎮 Gaming Applications: PUBG, Clash of Kings and Mobile Legends.

🛒 E-Commerce: AliExpress, Club Factory, Shein and Gearbest.

📱 Utility Applications: Truecaller, CamScanner and BeautyPlus.

🎥 Video & Live Streaming: TikTok, Zoom, Bigo Live and LiveMe.

🔐 Revised Social Media Policy

The Indian Army subsequently amended its social media guidelines in December 2025.

👁️ Instagram, X, YouTube and Quora: Restricted to passive viewing and information gathering.

💬 WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal and Skype: Permitted for exchanging general, unclassified information with known individuals.

💼 LinkedIn: Restricted to specified professional and employment-related purposes.

⚠️ Why Such Stringent Restrictions?

🕵️ Counter-Espionage: Preventing hostile intelligence agencies from targeting military personnel through digital platforms.

🍯 Honey Trapping: Reducing exposure to fraudulent identities and online recruitment attempts.

📍 Operational Security (OPSEC): Preventing inadvertent disclosure of sensitive military information.

📊 Data Security: Mitigating unauthorised collection of personal information and digital metadata.

🧠 Strategic Lens

Modern intelligence warfare extends far beyond conventional battlefields. A soldier's digital footprint can become a valuable intelligence resource for hostile agencies.

The Indian Army's restrictions reflect the growing importance of digital discipline, counter-intelligence awareness and information security within the armed forces.

In the age of digital espionage, operational security begins long before a soldier enters the battlefield.

text:
Section 17A of the Prevention of Corruption Act. Another Backdoor to Protect IAS-IPS Corruption

How do the powerful become more powerful and citizens more helpless in India? Look at how laws are repeatedly changed to protect the corrupts, while courts take years to decide their constitutionality.

In 1997 , the Supreme Court struck down the requirement of prior government permission to investigate senior bureaucrats.

The protection returned through Section 6A of the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act in 2003.

In 2014, a five-judge Constitution Bench, in Subramanian Swamy v. Director, CBI, unanimously struck down Section 6A as discriminatory and violative of Article 14. Why should senior bureaucrats enjoy protection from investigation merely because of their rank?

The protection was gone again.

But this all thirsty bureaucratic cartel  would not surrender so easily.

In 2018, Section 17A was inserted into the Prevention of Corruption Act.

It provides that no police officer shall conduct any enquiry, inquiry or investigation into an offence under the Act relating to a recommendation made or decision taken by a public servant in the discharge of official duties without previous approval from the competent government or authority.

Now understand where the biggest corruption takes place.

It is not merely the constable collecting money from truck drivers or the clerk taking bribes in a district Collectorate.

The biggest corruption happens on files, through decisions granting undue benefits, manipulating policies, awarding contracts, granting approvals and transferring public resources to private hands.

Can anyone think senior IAS and IPS officers personally collect bribes in cash? They have properties, villas, gold, investments, NGOs, and assets, even in foreign, held in the names of relatives, associates and others. 

It was already extraordinarily difficult to get IAS and IPS officers investigated. Can any common citizen get a DM investigated for mess in a district? Their cadres dominate administration, vigilance and the institutions that handle complaints. Complaints are buried.

But they do not want even a one-percent chance of being investigated.

Look at the recent Rajasthan villas case involving IAS officer Shikhar Agrawal and his IPS officer wife. The Anti-Corruption Bureau is investigating alleged irregularities involving dozens of villas and official decisions benefiting a private company. Agrawal approached the High Court to challenge even the government’s approval for investigation under Section 17A.

And investigations can themselves be managed within the same bureaucratic ecosystem. But the possibility of investigators discovering something still frightens them. It means more trouble, more exposure and more money spent protecting themselves.

The excuse for Section 17A was that honest officers need protection from harassment. Really? Who needs honest officers? They need loyal officers.

In January 2026, the Supreme Court again delivered a split verdict.

Justice B.V. Nagarathna held Section 17A unconstitutional, relying on the earlier Supreme Court judgments.

Justice K.V. Viswanathan upheld the provision with a requirement for independent scrutiny through the Lokpal or Lokayukta.

The matter went to a larger Bench, and Section 17A continues to operate.

Now compare how quickly protections for bureaucrats are created with what happens to laws intended to protect citizens.

The Whistle Blowers Protection Act was passed in 2014 but has never been brought into force. Have you see any haste to mandatory install cameras to police officers while duty or mandatory working CCTV cameras in police stations for protecting innocent citizens? Transparency and accountability laws are not implemented and left inoperative. 

The Lokpal Act originally required public servants to disclose assets and liabilities of themselves, their spouses and dependent children. Parliament amended Section 44 in 2016, removing those specific disclosure requirements and leaving the procedure to executive rules.

Ten years later, those promised rules are still awaited.

See the pattern?

This is how a corrupt and feudal system protects itself while citizens become increasingly powerless. Citizens are in illusion that this system is working for them. We are only their subjects whom they want to rule.

What kind of democracy makes it easier to protect a corrupt public servant from investigation than to protect a citizen who exposes corruption?

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

The Delhi High Court has ordered that the results of the All India Tennis Association (AITA) elections, scheduled for 27 November, be kept under sealed cover and not declared until further orders, after ruling that the interim committee acted without authority in appointing an Electoral Officer for the polls.

A bench of Acting Chief Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Sanjay Sharma passed the order on Thursday on a contempt plea filed by court-appointed Administrator Justice (Retd.) Gita Mittal.

Under the court's 27 April 2026 order, election powers rest solely with the Administrator. Until the next hearing, the committee is barred from taking major policy decisions and making financial transactions.

Justice Mittal was appointed after Davis Cuppers Somdev Devvarman and Purav Raja challenged the 2024 AITA polls under the National Sports Code. Her report stated that the interim committee had "ceased to exist" after it named a non-elected treasurer without her knowledge.

The matter will next be heard on 14 December.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

New Delhi, 1 July 2026

The UAE dirham has been pinned to the US dollar at exactly 3.6725 since 1997. The rate is not allowed to move. So can someone explain why this $100 payment lost a dollar to “currency conversion”?

A US customer paid $100 for a Dubai SaaS subscription. The merchant received $94.83 (AED 348.26). The missing $5.17 didn’t disappear. It was split along a chain of intermediaries you’ve never heard of.

Most people think a card payment is one transaction. It’s not. It’s a relay race between 8 parties, running on two parallel networks, each taking a different cut on a different timeline.

I traced a single $100 payment from the US to the UAE, end to end. Here’s what I found.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝟮 𝗻𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀 𝗿𝘂𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗯𝘆 𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲:

→ The info layer: ~2 seconds. Authorisation messages bouncing between the US issuer, the card network and the merchant’s processor. This is the part that flashes “Order paid ✓” on the merchant’s screen.

→ The money layer: days. On Stripe’s standard UAE schedule, the merchant gets paid out T+5 business days, with the USD→AED conversion buried in the middle.

Your checkout feels instant. The money is still in flight, and that quiet conversion step in the middle is where the margin hides.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 $𝟱.𝟭𝟳 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘄𝗲𝗻𝘁:

1️⃣ You: $100 leaves your account
2️⃣ US issuing bank (Chase / Bank of America): authorises, takes interchange −$1.80 (cross-border online: 1.60–1.98%)
3️⃣ Card network (Visa / Mastercard): ≈−$0.80 in scheme and cross-border fees (estimate)
4️⃣ FX / currency conversion: −$1.00, Stripe’s 1% markup on a rate fixed at 3.6725
5️⃣ Stripe: −$1.57, the rest of its 2.9% + 1% international card + AED 1 fee
6️⃣ VAT (UAE · FTA): $0 if the merchant has a UAE VAT number (otherwise 5% on Stripe’s fees, ≈$0.26, recoverable)
7️⃣ Merchant’s UAE bank: no fee, AED payout T+5 business days
8️⃣ UAE SaaS merchant: receives AED 348.26 (~$94.83)
Total: 4.9% + AED 1 gone before the merchant sees a dirham. And the US customer may also pay a 0–3% foreign transaction fee to their own bank, on top.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗲𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱𝗻’𝘁 𝗲𝘅𝗶𝘀𝘁:

In India, the biggest cut was a ~2.3% FX spread, and you could almost justify it: the rupee floats, so someone is carrying real currency risk.

The dirham doesn’t float. It’s hard-pegged. The rate literally cannot move outside 3.672–3.673. There is no FX risk to price.

And yet the “currency conversion” line is still there: 1% at Stripe. On a pegged currency, that isn’t risk. It’s margin with a story attached. The proof: price the same product in AED and that line disappears. The merchant keeps $95.83 instead of $94.83.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁’𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗯𝘆 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻:

The customer sees 1 actor (their bank). The merchant sees 2 (Stripe and their bank). Everything in between is invisible.

The next generation of payment infrastructure isn’t trying to add another intermediary. It’s trying to delete most of them

Supreme Court: In a matter concerning the growing menace of digital arrest scams and other cyber frauds, a three-Judge Bench of Surya Kant, CJ with Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana, JJ., emphasised that the regulatory measures proposed by Reserve Bank of India (RBI) must mandate financial institutions to indemnify victims and pay compensation not less than the amount lost, where the fraud is established to have occurred due to their failure to exercise due diligence. 

The Court further underscored the need for preventive safeguards, including temporarily suspending suspicious transactions, automatically intimating the nearest police station and physically verifying such transactions to ascertain their genuineness.

The present matter concerns the growing menace of digital arrest scams and other cyber frauds. The Amicus Curiae, vide note dated 14 October 2026, had suggested various measures and consequential directions to address the issue. In response, the learned Attorney General for India, on behalf of the Union of India, placed a note dated 28 October 2026 on record, suggesting certain directions.

The Court, while expressing its inclination to issue appropriate directions in light of the suggestions made by the learned Amicus Curiae and the Union of India, considered it appropriate, in the first instance, to examine the Reserve Bank of India (Know Your Customer) Amendment Directions, 2026, proposed to be notified by 30 November 2026 and operationalised by 31 December 2026.

The Court reiterated and emphasised that the regulatory measures proposed by RBI must mandate and incorporate suitable provisions requiring financial institutions to indemnify victims of digital arrest scams and other cyber frauds and pay suitable compensation not less than the amount lost by the customer, where it is established that the fraud or crime occurred due to the failure of the financial institution to exercise due diligence in preventing or reporting the act/incident.

The Court further emphasised the need for preventive safeguards to be mandated for every financial institution. These may include temporarily suspending unusual or suspicious transactions inconsistent with the account’s past transaction history, automatically intimating such transactions to the nearest police station and subsequently physically verifying the reported transactions to ascertain their genuineness.

The Court allowed IA No. 167477/2026 (application for intervention), permitting the applicant(s) to intervene in the matter.

To ensure effective implementation of the regulatory measures proposed by RBI, as well as the directions issued by the Court, RBI was directed to submit a list of all authorised financial institutions before the Court on the next date of hearing.

Further, all law enforcement agencies in the States and Union Territories were directed to submit the status of the FIRs registered thus far in connection with digital arrest scam cases, details of the resultant investigations undertaken and suggestions for appropriate measures for the prevention, detection and prosecution of such cases. The Directors General of Police of all States and Union Territories were directed to ensure compliance with these directions. The information furnished to the Court shall simultaneously be forwarded to the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C).
Additionally, WhatsApp LLC (a Meta Company) and other intermediaries concerned were directed to apprise the Court of the measures they propose to undertake to prevent digital arrest scams and related cybercrimes. They were also directed to simultaneously submit their proposals to the I4C.

#India: COURT DENIES KETAN PAREKH PERMISSION FOR 91-DAY FOREIGN HOLIDAY

A special securities court in Mumbai has rejected former stockbroker Ketan Parekh's request to travel to nine countries for a three-month family vacation.

Parekh, whose name became associated with India's major 2000–2001 stock market scandal, sought permission to visit Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, the UAE, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Denmark and Switzerland between December 20, 2026, and March 20, 2027.

At a hearing on November 20, Special SEBI Judge R. M. Jadhav ruled that granting unrestricted permission for such an extended period would not serve India's national or economic interests.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) opposed the application, alleging that Parekh had previously misused permission to travel abroad and had engaged in further securities-related misconduct involving confidential market information.

SEBI also raised concerns over an outstanding order concerning ₹27 crore in alleged unlawful gains.

The court acknowledged the right to travel abroad but concluded that the risks associated with a 91-day absence justified refusing this particular request.

The ruling does not determine liability in the ongoing securities proceedings.

Many journalists, politicians, and creators in India are facing similar issues; accounts being suspended, posts removed, or visibility reduced with little transparency or meaningful recourse.

These actions often happen under two parallel mechanisms of India’s Information Technology Act, 2000.

Section 69A allows the Government to issue blocking orders on broad grounds such as national security or public order. However, these orders are usually confidential, and affected users often receive neither notice nor a copy of the blocking order, making it difficult to challenge them.

Separately, Section 79(3)(b) allows authorities to pressure platforms to remove content by threatening loss of “safe harbour” protections if platforms fail to comply with government or court directions. In practice, this creates strong incentives for platforms to over-comply.

The lack of transparency around these processes raises serious concerns for due process, free expression, and accountability.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

It is so painfully obvious that using an AI notetaker should not waive privilege. 

The fact that a law firm could hire someone to take notes on the call while maintaining privilege answers the question. We settled this with email decades ago.

Clients should always have the option to not have their calls recorded - but the purpose of privilege is to allow clients to speak freely. The idea that using technology to transcribe and analyze means the information is not confidential...doesn't make sense. 

People want increased access to justice, faster service, and lower fees. AI notetakers will help with that! 

Yes, you need to have "sufficient protections" that ensure the AI providers are not using the data for their own purposes and that the data is secure. It's a legitimate discussion - and we should debate which protections are enough. But this is a solvable problem. Bar associations could easily create safe harbor provisions that providers could certify they comply with. 

Part of why this will take so long to get to the right answer is that this is an issue where many lawyers actually enjoy the debate. Many judges will opine about the true nature and historical roots of privilege. They will debate definitions and look at many particular contractual terms to decide whether they are "sufficiently protective."

This is all instead of just helping to educate lawyers about how to use products safely.

In the end, I am 100% confident we will get to a point where it's widely accepted that people are using AI notetakers and it doesn't violate privilege. It's frustrating it's going to take so long.

This claim conflates three different systems and the notices themselves disprove it.

Meta stopped removing content solely for being manipulated media in July 2024. Its policy now is to label AI content and keep it up unless it violates another policy like voter interference, harassment, or incitement. A genuine photo is not manipulated media, so a deepfake filter has no reason to remove it globally.

What people are seeing is not global removal. It is geo-restriction: "unavailable in India" under India's IT Rules, visible outside India. Meta reports local-law restrictions separately from Community Standards removals. If it were a deepfake removal, it would be gone everywhere, with a 'Community Standards' notice.

Yes, automation is involved. But it is legal-requirement automation, not deepfake detection. Since Feb 20, 2026, Rule 4(4) requires platforms to use automated tools against content exactly identical to content already taken down under a court order or govt notice. That system can over-block by matching a real photo to a previously restricted file. That is identical-content matching under Indian law, not a classifier deciding a real photo is fake.

The @Arappor Iyakkam reel proves the point. Its notice did not say an automated filter fired. It said: legal request received, reviewed, legal and human rights assessment done, then restricted where it goes against local law. And the content was a protest song about tender policy, not a deepfake.

text:
If an agent drafts email that goes out under your name, write every unverified fact into the body as a visible placeholder that blocks the send. A warning in the chat window alone does not do that job.

I work in wind energy operations, and an always-on ops agent runs my email desk. It drafts, and it sends only after I give an explicit send command on the latest version it has shown me. The rule below exists because of one email I had to correct.

What happened

A draft stated a third party's commitment as settled. The warning to confirm it first sat only in the chat. The body of the email said it as fact. I sent the body as written, and a correction email had to follow.

The placeholder

The body now contains only facts with a written source. Anything unsupported is written inline as a visible placeholder: "pending written confirmation from X about Y".

A draft that contains a placeholder cannot be sent. It also cannot be handed to me to send myself.

The chat note stayed in the chat when the email went out. A placeholder sits inside the draft, so the open question goes wherever the draft goes, and the send stays blocked until somebody answers it in writing.

The receipt list

The second half is about my own review. I could not tell at a glance which statements in a draft were grounded and which were inferred.

Every email the agent drafts reaches me as a confirmation package: send method, To, Cc, subject and the full body. The package also lists each key third-party claim with source, date and original wording. Claims without a source go in a separate "to confirm" list.

So I check a short evidence table and do not have to re-read whole threads to see what a draft rests on. A check I would suggest for each row: does the original wording say what the draft says?

The incidents behind the other rules

Two more rules came out of incidents in my own drafts.

The first was a fuzzy answer completed in my favor. The reply said "we can provide data". The agent filled that in as a formal signed report. In reality only internal data was possible. Put that claim next to its original wording and the gap would show in one row: the draft says signed report, the source says data.

The rule that goes with it: if the other side did not say who does it, what exactly, in what form and by when, the agent asks a follow-up question. It does not pick the reading that suits me best. Completing text is what a language model does, so this rule marks a place where mine has to stop and ask.

The second was a statement stretched. A narrow statement from the other side was expanded into a broader permission and written with "we understand this is acceptable, let us know otherwise" phrasing. That phrasing is banned now. Quotes keep their original meaning, and anything that needs the other party's agreement is written as an explicit question. Until they answer, their agreement is still pending.

What it costs

Speed, mostly. A draft with a placeholder waits, by design, until the answer exists in writing. The order of work changes too: before I commit externally to a method, a lead time, a quantity or a price, the written confirmation from whoever has to execute it comes first. Once, the recipient was told about a deliverable before the party who had to deliver it had confirmed. I would rather wait than write another correction email.

Where it breaks

A receipt shows that someone wrote something. A party can confirm in writing and still be wrong.

The weak point, I think, is that the agent decides what counts as a key third-party claim: one it does not recognize gets no receipt and no placeholder. So the receipt list is a guide to where to read hardest, and the body still has to be read.

The version to copy

1. Body: only facts with a written source.
2. Unsupported claim: write it in the body as "pending written confirmation from X about Y". Never only as a note in chat.
3. A draft with a placeholder cannot be sent, and cannot be handed to you to send.
4. Vague answer (no who, what, form or date): ask a follow-up question. Do not complete it.
5. Needs their agreement: ask an explicit question. No "we understand this is acceptable".

Good morning, happy Sunday, and welcome to the weekly update. This week's topics:

1. My Two Cents: False Alarms at the Maritime Centre
2. Floating Dock for Fire Boat 1
3. New Rescue Boat
4. Electric Vehicles
5. HRFE is Hiring: EVT

---
1. Common false alarms are something HRFE, and I assume many other fire departments, deal with. Smoke from Brothers Meats on Agricola, the crematorium on King, or flames from the Bedford Sewage plant are all common false alarms for HRFE. A report of "smoke", which is actually steam, coming from a mechanical room on the middle floors of the Maritime Centre is one of HRFE's most prominent false alarms. Here's my two cents on the issue.

I think it is time that they take a look at how these calls are getting dispatched. Every time this call comes in, it gets paged out as a full first alarm structure fire assignment, which means three engines, an aerial, a chief, a tactical unit, and a platoon captain. All units going code one, lights and sirens.

At a certain point, in my opinion, given the very specific and predictable fact pattern, the risk of this being a fire does not dictate sending seven units code one to this call. Yes, I understand, everything is treated as a fire until proven otherwise. However, there's a reason backup units go code three to fire alarms activated. The risk, in my view, doesn't dictate all units starting out code one. I would argue a single caller ten blocks away reporting they can see white steam from the mechanical room for the sixth time in a couple months is a condition that warrants HRFE adjusting the response in some manner.

Another item that has been raised is fines. My understanding is that generally the building is not being issued an Alarm Systems Notification (ASN) for these types of calls, so I highly doubt the building is being fined. I'm OK with that - it isn't the Maritime Centre's fault if someone calls this condition in from ten blocks away.  That's not really what ASNs are for. In terms of other remedies, I don't know what jurisdiction the department would have to ask or order the building to make some type of change to the steam production. I doubt HRFE has much authority to order that. So, given that  I don't think they can force the building into anything, and given that they can't stop people from calling this in, I think the department needs to take a close look at adjusting responses to this particular fact pattern to align with the potential risk.

I don't have a strong opinion about what the response should be, but seven units going code one to these calls seems quite frankly ridiculous. My own view is it should probably be a single-unit response for an investigation call, unless the information from the caller differs from the typical fact pattern. However, my main point is they need to review this response and not keep simply sending a full first alarm no matter how predictable the outcome is. This same false alarm with the exact same fact pattern has come in at least two dozen times in the last couple of years, needlessly tying up resources that could be available for other calls.

Some may not agree with this, and I can already hear people saying "well there's no way they'll adjust the response because what if that one time, it is a fire". Well, to be honest, I think this is an invalid argument. First off, by that logic, why not send a full first alarm to every automatic alarm? There's a reason one unit goes code one and the rest go code three on an automatic alarm. There's a reason one unit gets assigned for a generic "smoke in the area" type calls, etc. Those responses are generated proportionate to the risk. Secondly, every one of these Maritime Centre calls is coming in with a very specific fact pattern: one caller, far away from the building, "smoke" around the 10th floor, etc. If the fact pattern comes in differently, of course sending a full first alarm might make sense. However,  sending a full first alarm response with everybody going code one is not a proportionate response to that one same predictable fact pattern, in my opinion. Check it out? Absolutely. Seven units code one? I cannot follow that logic.

Feel free to disagree, but since people have asked, there's my two cents on the Maritime Centre.

---
2. HRM has issued a tender for a floating dock for Fire Boat 1. It sounds like this is going to be installed in the same or a similar position to where the Fire Boat is docked currently, at Alderney Marina. The tender calls for a floating dock setup with lighting and a power connection, I believe for the boat. Having discussed it with a couple of people, it sounds like this is something crews were hoping for and that it will improve FB01 operations. Good to see

---
3. HRM has also issued a tender for a new rescue boat. There isn't a ton of detail in the tender documents. It states they're looking for a 16' polyethylene boat for rescue purposes. It doesn't even say explicitly it is for HRFE, although I think that is a fairly safe assumption given it is for rescue purposes. I stand to be corrected but I think 16' would make it slightly larger than most of the Zodiac boats currently in the field (Rescue Boats 6, 9, 14, 23, 26, 38, 42, 45). Given the specs they have listed, I'm fairly confident this is a lake boat, not a harbour boat, and also there's no indication it will have any firefighting capacity. Will share more details when I get them.

---
4. The province of NS has developed an electric vehicle registry. The fire department has an obvious interest in electric vehicles given that they present different challenges than traditional vehicles. Here are some statistics from the registry:

- As of January 2024, there are 10,549 electric vehicles in Nova Scotia
- As a share of total vehicles, this is still relatively small, at 1.3%
- 6,852 or 65% of these vehicles are registered in HRM
- 73% are three years old or less
- The most common manufacturer is Tesla, at 38.5%, followed by Hyundai (21.3%), and Chevrolet (12.4%)

---
5. HRFE is hiring a mechanic, also known as an EVT (Emergency Vehicle Technician). You can see the job posting here: https://t.co/YKRSrToWD9

---
That's all for this week. Have a great Sunday!

Section 6(4) of the DPDP Act gives a Data Principal, the person the data is about, the right to withdraw consent at any time, and withdrawing must be comparable in ease to giving consent. Section 6(6) then requires the Data Fiduciary, the business that decides why and how the data is processed, to stop processing within a reasonable time and to make its Data Processors stop too, unless a law requires or authorises the processing.

Business Standard reported on 18 November 2026 that companies are mapping where personal data flows for this reason. The report says a withdrawal made in an app can leave the data in use in a data warehouse, an analytics platform or an automated pipeline that never received the update. It also says protection has to cover AI prompts, retrieval, agent memory and connected tools. Rishi Agrawal of TeamLease RegTech told the paper that the harder task is making a withdrawal take effect in every system that uses the data.

text:
Starlink has an Indian license, 20 ground stations on Indian soil, and a promise to keep Indian user data in India. What it doesn't have is permission to switch on.

Thousands of Indian villages still have no 4G. In the Northeast alone, more than 1,800 had no mobile signal of any kind as of February, most of them in Arunachal Pradesh. These are the places satellite internet is built for: mountain villages, islands, flood zones, anywhere a tower or a fiber line takes years and a lot of money to arrive.

Starlink has done what India asked. It got its telecom license in June 2025 and space regulator approval a month later. It built India-specific security controls, agreed to keep data local, and has been reporting the names, addresses and coordinates of its test terminals to the government every two weeks. It operates in more than 150 countries. In India it still can't sell a single subscription, and the company is now talking about early 2027.

New Delhi says nobody is being singled out, since Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio's satellite venture are stuck at the same stage. I believe that, and I don't think it helps. When three licensed operators, two of them backed by India's biggest telecom groups, can't clear security review after more than a year of trials, that tells you the process has no deadline. It doesn't tell you it's thorough.

The security concerns are real. Indian agencies have been rattled by smuggled terminals turning up in border areas, and India is entitled to lawful interception, local data storage and an emergency shutoff. Starlink has already signed up for all of it. The answer to a misused terminal is enforcement, not keeping the service dark for everyone who would use it legally.

Elon Musk has been blunt, calling the delay "a crime against the people of India" and asking, "Is Ambani the real boss of India?" You don't need to buy the whole oligarch theory to see his point. Reliance spent months lobbying for spectrum auctions that would have favored deep-pocketed incumbents. The government sided with Starlink on that one, which is to its credit. Now it needs to finish the job.

India can keep every security power it wants and still let a kid in Arunachal get online. Right now it's choosing not to.
